subject: Dedicated capacity options for Lumina Health — cluster sizing, min GPUs, and ramp orchestration
messages:
From: Sofia Ivanova <sofia.ivanova@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Cho <alex.cho@luminahealth.com>, Priya Rao <priya.rao@luminahealth.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>

Subject: Dedicated capacity options for Lumina Health — cluster sizing, min GPUs, and ramp orchestration

Hi Alex / Priya,

Per our call today I wanted to put a concise set of options on paper for Lumina's dedicated reservation so your procurement and infra teams can evaluate trade-offs. Attached is a workbook with per-GPU throughput estimates and a short PDF that summarizes pricing anchors. Below is the recommended approach and the operational knobs we suggest you consider.

Executive summary (short):
- We recommend a two-phase onramp: a controlled pilot (validate prompts, caching behavior) then a capacity ramp to production.
- Three candidate reservation profiles (pilot → production → peak burst) with min-GPU guarantees and explicit burst capacity.

Recommended capacity profiles (example hardware = NVIDIA A100 / H100 compatible):
1) Pilot (conservative): 8 GPUs total, min guarantee 4 GPUs.
   - Purpose: smoke test integration, validate latency SLOs and KV/prefix caching.
   - Expected steady QPS: ~120 small-text req/s (tail dependent on prompt sizes).
   - Activation window: 2–4 weeks from signing.

2) Core production (recommended starting contract): 24 GPUs total, min guarantee 12 GPUs.
   - Purpose: multi-service production traffic with predictable performance.
   - Expected steady QPS: ~350–420 small-text req/s, with room for batching.
   - SLA considerations: 99.9% uptime for dedicated cluster lanes; cost anchors in attached workbook.

3) Scale / Peak (for bursty or heavy embeddings): up to 64 GPUs (burst pool), min guarantee 32 GPUs (if you want absolute runway).
   - Purpose: handle model upgrades, heavy embedding/semantic search indexing jobs, and large parallel fine-tune workloads.
   - Burst strategy: a quotaable burst pool + short-term prewarmed lanes to reduce cold-start token latency.

Ramp orchestration (proposed timeline):
- Week 0: Sign + reserved slot provisioning request. Reserve baseline nodes and activate network/VPC peering.
- Week 1–3: Pilot activation (8 GPU lane). Validate inference pipelines, KV caching, and egress rules.
- Month 1–2: Scale to Core production (24 GPU lane) with staged traffic cutover (canary → 25% → 50% → 100%).
- Month 3–6: Optional scale to Peak (64 GPUs) depending on usage growth; we recommend agreed triggers (QPS or token burn thresholds) for automatic scaling.

Minimum guarantees and flexibility:
- We recommend a contract with a 50% minimum guarantee clause for the first 3 months (e.g., min 12 GPUs if you order 24). This reduces your committed spend while giving us enough runway to reserve racks.
- Add-on: short-term burst credits (30% of base capacity) that can be consumed for seasonal indexing or model releases.

Operational notes and fallbacks: 
- Warm-start buffer: we prewarm subset of instances for the first 2 hours of a release to avoid high tail latency for new model variants.
- Fallback runtime: if dedicated capacity is impacted, Redwood will auto-route to a compatible hosted tier (degraded SLOs) to keep critical traffic live.
- Observability: token-level cost dashboards and per-model latency heatmaps will be available in the Console.

Pricing anchors and SOW next steps:
- See attached workbook for per-GPU monthly rates, effective per-token costs under batching assumptions, and a few sample burn forecasts.
- If you confirm target QPS and preferred baseline (Pilot vs Core), we can issue an SOW and a staged payment schedule.

Ask / next steps:
- Can you confirm which of the three profiles you want to evaluate first (Pilot / Core / Scale)?
- Please share the names for the procurement contact and preferred legal cadence.
- Are there any hard constraints for activation windows (e.g., must be live by Oct 1)?

Thanks — happy to jump back on a 30-min slot to walk the workbook.

Best,
Sofia Ivanova

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity options for Lumina Health — cluster sizing, min GPUs, and ramp orchestration

Thanks Sofia — this is very helpful. A couple of clarifying questions from infra/procurement before we loop in legal: 

1) Hardware: we are evaluating H100 for the production lane (better perf/dollar for our embeddings). Are the per-GPU numbers in the workbook for A100 or H100? If A100, can you provide a quick delta for H100?

2) Burst / preemption: our indexing jobs can be huge and occasionally preempt other workloads in our current setup. For the burst pool you propose — will those be dedicated (isolated racks) or shared across customers? We need to understand isolation risk.

3) Minimum guarantee: procurement will push for the smallest commitment possible. Is a month-to-month with a 2-week activation SLA and conversion credits to seasonal burst credits an option?

4) Cold-start tail: our latency SLO for the UI is 200ms P95 on short prompts. How much of that is realistic when a model upgrade happens and all caches are cold?

Alex
VP Engineering, Lumina Health
alex.cho@luminahealth.com

Alex — quick answers to the infra questions here, happy to expand on a call: 

1) Hardware delta (A100 vs H100): the workbook baseline is priced on A100-equivalent. H100 gives roughly 1.6x throughput for many transformer decoding workloads (and even better for FP8 quantized paths). If you want I can generate an H100 column in the workbook — it typically increases per-GPU list price but lowers tokens-per-dollar in sustained workloads. (Attached: ben_cost_illustrator.csv — quick scenario outputs.)

2) Burst pool isolation: we offer two burst models — a "soft-burst" shared pool (lower cost, higher variability) and a "hard-burst" reserved rack option (higher cost, strict isolation). Given Lumina's sensitivity, I recommend the hard-burst reserved racks for indexing jobs that must not be preempted. We can map those to a different failure domain to minimize noisy neighbor risk.

3) Minimum guarantee flexibility: we can structure a 3-month ramp contract with a reduced first-month guarantee (25% of target) and a crediting mechanism: unused months convert to burst credits that you can spend within the first 90 days following the term. Month-to-month after initial ramp is possible but will change pricing and SLO commitments; procurement typically prefers a 3-month initial term for operational predictability.

4) Cold-start tail: with warm-start buffers and prefix/KV cache priming, we observe P95 degradation limited to ~1.5–2x baseline on immediate first requests after a model rollout. For a 200ms P95 baseline, a worst-case warmup spike could be 300–400ms P95 for short windows (minutes). We strongly recommend staged canary rollout + prewarming for any major release to stay under your SLOs.

If you'd like I can schedule a 30-min technical deep-dive with our infra lead (Karthik) to go over H100 scenarios and the rack placement topology.

—Ben
